paper_metadata.title: LatentQGAN: A Hybrid QGAN with Classical Convolutional Autoencoder

summary: The paper presents LatentQGAN, a hybrid gate-based QGAN for MNIST image generation that compresses 28×28 images into a 5×8 latent space using a classical convolutional autoencoder, then trains a 5-subgenerator quantum model with 4 qubits per sub-generator and 7 variational layers. Experiments were run on a simulator and IBM Eagle (2048 shots, 140 parameters), with best Frechet Distance typically reached between 350 and 700 iterations and an optimal iteration count reported as 490; the paper reports improved image quality over prior QGAN baselines but does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum-classical GAN for MNIST image generation using a classical convolutional autoencoder to compress images into a latent space, followed by a quantum generator and classical discriminator trained on the latent representation; evaluated on simulator and IBM Eagle quantum hardware for classes 0, 5, and 9.

algorithm.variant: LatentQGAN hybrid QGAN with classical convolutional autoencoder
algorithm.ansatz: Parameterized quantum circuit with rotation gates and sequential CZ entangling layers; partial measurement with ancillary qubits
algorithm.convergence_criteria: optimal number of iterations determined empirically; training evaluated up to 1000 iterations, with best FD typically between 350 and 700 iterations and optimal iteration count reported as 490 for all 10 MNIST classes
algorithm.parameter_initialization: same initial parameters as simulator training for quantum-computer run; random noise vectors sampled uniformly

problem_formulation.encoding_details: random noise vector encoded by rotation gates; latent representation normalized line-by-line to match generator constraints; each of 5 sub-generators produces one row of the 5x8 latent space
problem_formulation.objective_function: GAN minimax objective with binary cross-entropy loss for generator/discriminator; autoencoder trained with mean squared error reconstruction loss
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: line-wise normalization of encoder latent output; partial measurement/post-selection on ancillary qubits to obtain generator output probabilities

problem_instance.description: MNIST handwritten digit image generation in latent space; results reported for classes 0, 5, and 9

dataset_specification.description: 28x28 grayscale handwritten digits; classes 0-9; evaluation focused on classes 0, 5, and 9

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: images compressed by convolutional autoencoder into normalized latent space of dimension 5 x 8
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Frechet Distance (FD) used to compare generated samples with ground truth; simulator and real-hardware results compared; quantum-computer results obtained from a single run using identical noise vectors and initial parameters as simulator trainings

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise on IBM quantum computer

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: autoencoder trained first on all classes together; latent representation normalized line-by-line before QGAN training
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: decoder reconstructs images from generated latent vectors; FD computed for evaluation

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: FD improves up to mid-training then visually decays after about 700 iterations

speedup_claims.conditions: to achieve comparable results / minimal FD on the reported MNIST classes
speedup_claims.caveats: Claim is based on iteration count, not wall-clock time; comparison is against a simulator-based MosaiQ result and the paper does not provide a full matched experimental protocol.

speedup_claims.conditions: for the reported LatentQGAN configuration versus comparable classical or prior QGAN models
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states this as a resource reduction claim; exact per-baseline parameter counts are not fully enumerated in the text.
No asymptotic quantum advantage or formal speedup is proven.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No asymptotic speedup or crossover analysis is provided; the experiment uses 20 qubits total (5 sub-generators × 4 qubits) and 2048 shots on IBM Eagle.
limiting_factors: Classical baselines are competitive or better in the reported comparisons
Training requires many iterations (best FD typically between 350 and 700; optimal 490)

notes: num_qubits inferred as 20 from five quantum circuits with 4 qubits each (5 x 4) described in the experimental details; the paper also states the circuits can be parallelized on a 127-qubit IBM Eagle processor.
hardware.type reported as a real quantum computer on IBM Eagle; mapped to real_qpu_superconducting.
speedup_order not explicitly characterized asymptotically; only empirical performance improvements are reported.
The paper reports empirical image-quality comparisons against QPatchGAN, MosaiQ, LatentGAN, and RandomDecoder, but does not establish a practical quantum advantage.
Results are described as competitive on simulator and real hardware, but no rigorous advantage claim is demonstrated.
